title: Disease Containment, Testing Handoff & Reconstructable Records

content.overview: A specialist response must preserve both biological containment and information integrity. The record should let a qualified reviewer reconstruct what was observed, what moved, what was held, what was sampled/tested, what decisions were authorized and what remains unresolved.

vocabulary.definition: A temporary or ongoing control used to limit spread while diagnosis, testing or disposition is resolved.
A documented sequence showing specimen identity, collection, transfer, receipt and handling.
A traceable correction that preserves the original record and documents what changed, when and why.

sections.title: Contain first when spread consequence warrants it
sections.body: A suspect disease or HLVd finding may justify limiting movement of plants, tools or personnel while evidence is strengthened. Containment is a risk-control action, not proof of cause.

sections.title: Testing handoff must preserve identity
sections.body: Sample records should tie the specimen to plant/lot/location, collection time, collector, reason for test and laboratory/method result. Uncertain identity or chain-of-custody gaps reduce how confidently a result can support disposition.

sections.title: Separate facts, interpretation and authority
sections.body: Record direct observations, hypotheses, test results, actions taken, authorization source and unresolved follow-up separately. Do not rewrite earlier evidence to make the final diagnosis appear inevitable.

workedExamples: A positive laboratory result tied to a clearly identified donor plant and chain-of-custody record supports a much stronger containment/disposition decision than an unlabeled screenshot of a result.
commonMistakes: Discarding the original observation after the diagnosis changes.
Recording containment as if it proves infection.
Using a test result when sample identity cannot be reconstructed.
content.practicalApplication: Complete a mock disease incident record from first observation through containment, sample handoff, result, authorized disposition and next-shift follow-up.
content.summary: Disease control depends on both containment and trustworthy evidence. Reconstructable identity, sampling, testing, decisions and corrections are part of biosecurity.
